name: Ammonia
title: Ammonia in Cleaning Products: Safety, Fumes & the Bleach Rule — IngredientIQ
description: Ammonia is the streak-free ingredient in glass cleaners and a strong degreaser. It's safe diluted and ventilated but produces toxic chloramine gas if mixed with bleach. What to know.
subtitle: The sharp smell in classic glass cleaner. Harmless enough diluted — as long as it never meets bleach.
quickAnswer: Household ammonia (ammonium hydroxide) is a strong alkaline cleaner that cuts grease and dries without streaks, which is why it's in glass and multi-surface cleaners. At consumer concentrations (typically 1–10%) it's safe with ventilation. It is a potent respiratory and eye irritant in enclosed spaces, and mixing it with bleach — including cleaning cat urine, which contains ammonia, with bleach — produces chloramine gas. Never use ammonia and bleach products in the same session.
foundInShort: Glass cleaner, multi-surface sprays, floor cleaners, oven cleaner
mainConcern: Respiratory irritation; toxic gas with bleach
whatItIs: Ammonia is a gas (NH3) that dissolves in water to form ammonium hydroxide, a strongly alkaline solution. Household ammonia sold as a cleaner is usually 5–10%; the amount in a ready-to-use glass cleaner is often under 1%.
It also occurs naturally — it's in urine, fertiliser, and the smell of a neglected litter box — which matters for the mixing rule below.
whatItDoes: As a strong base it saponifies grease, turning it into a soap that rinses away, which makes it effective on stovetops, ovens, and oily glass. It evaporates completely, so it leaves no film or streaks — the reason it became the classic window-cleaner ingredient.
It is not a disinfectant. Ammonia cleans but doesn't reliably kill bacteria or viruses, which is where the temptation to add bleach comes from.
safety: Ammonia's toxicity is about concentration and air. Diluted household products used with a window open cause at most mild irritation. Concentrated ammonia, or diluted ammonia used in a closed bathroom, irritates the eyes, nose, throat, and lungs; people with asthma are more sensitive. Splashes of concentrated solution can burn skin and eyes.

The mixing hazard is the real risk. Ammonia + sodium hypochlorite (bleach) forms chloramine gases, which cause coughing, shortness of breath, chest pain, and at high exposure, pulmonary oedema. It doesn't take deliberate mixing: cleaning a litter tray or a urine-soaked carpet with bleach produces the same reaction, because urine contains ammonia. So does using a glass cleaner and then a bleach spray on the same surface.
Ammonia isn't carcinogenic and doesn't accumulate; the body produces and excretes it naturally. Environmental impact is low at household volumes.
whoShouldAvoid: Never use in the same room or session as bleach products
Don't clean urine (pet or human) with bleach; use an enzymatic or ammonia-based cleaner instead, or clean the urine fully first
People with asthma or COPD — use ammonia-free glass cleaners
On brass, aluminium, or marble, which it can damage

regulatory.status: Permitted in consumer cleaners. Labelling governed by the Federal Hazardous Substances Act; concentrated products require warnings. OSHA workplace exposure limit 50 ppm (8-hour).
Permitted. Solutions above 5% classified as corrosive and toxic to aquatic life; require hazard labelling and child-resistant closures at higher concentrations.
Permitted; Consumer Chemicals and Containers Regulations govern labelling.

commonProducts: Glass and window cleaners (many, though ammonia-free versions are common now)
Some hair dyes (as an alkaliser — a different use)
alternatives: Vinegar-and-water for glass (streak-free, but never with bleach either — it makes chlorine gas)
Enzymatic cleaners for urine and pet messes
Baking soda paste for oven grease

faqs.q: What happens if you mix ammonia and bleach?
faqs.a: Chloramine gas forms immediately. Symptoms — coughing, watery eyes, chest tightness — start within minutes. Leave the room, ventilate, and call poison control if you have breathing symptoms. In a closed space this can be a medical emergency.

faqs.q: Can I use bleach to clean cat urine?
faqs.a: Not until the urine is completely removed. Urine contains ammonia, and bleach on it produces chloramine. Use an enzymatic cleaner, which also removes the odour bleach can't.
No. It's a cleaner and degreaser but doesn't kill germs reliably. If you need to disinfect, clean with ammonia first, rinse, then use a disinfectant separately — never bleach in the same session.

The smell is your warning system: ammonia is detectable well below harmful levels. If it's making your eyes water or you're coughing, the concentration is too high for the space — open windows and step out.
